title: Before and after
job: Time clauses: while, until, since, already, not yet
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: cum IS TWO WORDS WITH ONE SPELLING, AND THE INDEX CAN ONLY HOLD ONE NOTE. L1-M7 taught cum plus the ABLATIVE for 'with' — cum magistrō — and owns that key. This module writes cum plus a SUBJUNCTIVE for 'when'. Same four letters, two grammars, and first occurrence wins in the index — so every cum row in this module carries a note naming BOTH readings and saying which is which. The signal is what follows: a case means 'with', a mood means 'when'. This is the only remedy available, because withholding the second reading was possible for quod, quam and ut and is not possible here — a time clause is this module's job.

A cum CLAUSE IN THE PAST TAKES M3's SHAPES AND HAS NOTHING HYPOTHETICAL ABOUT IT. cum vēnisset is 'when he had come' — the pluperfect subjunctive; cum aeger essem is 'when I was ill' — the imperfect subjunctive. Both are facts. M3 opened those forms for counterfactuals, so a learner who met them in a module about regrets will read a time clause as a hypothetical unless told otherwise. The mood is what the conjunction requires, not what the meaning implies.

THE IMPERFECT IS WRITTEN HERE BEFORE M8 OPENS IT, AND THE NOTES SAY SO. A cum clause about the past needs a past beside it, and the perfect would make every sentence in this module a single finished event. So gaudēbam, labōrābam and exspectābam appear, three of them, as shapes this course has not yet taught properly — M8 is where the tense is explained, and this module borrows it rather than pretending it is old.

dōnec TAKES THE INDICATIVE FOR A FACT AND A SUBJUNCTIVE FOR A THING STILL TO COME. dōnec vēnit, exspectāvī — 'I waited until he came', which happened. dōnec veniat, exspectābō — 'I shall wait until he comes', which has not. So this module has two time conjunctions with opposite defaults, which is M4's quamquam-and-licet problem on a different pair and has the same answer: learn each with its construction.

exspectō TAKES A PLAIN OBJECT AND NO 'FOR'. 'I wait for him' is eum exspectō — the fifth construction in this course where an English preposition has nowhere to attach, after raedā, hōrā, auxilium rogō and mūsicam audiō. English 'expect' is the same word and has kept the transitivity.

iam IS 'ALREADY' AND 'NOW', AND THE TENSE DECIDES. iam vēnit with a perfect is 'he has already come'; iam labōrō with a present is 'now I work'. So English's whole 'has … already' construction is one small word in front of a tense the course has had since L1-M5. And nōn iam is 'NO LONGER' — two taught words making a third meaning, which is the cheapest new thing in the module.

nōndum IS nōn AND dum WELDED TOGETHER, and it is the sixth word in this course with a negative inside it: nōlō, mālō, negō, nisi, nesciō, nōndum. By now that is a habit of the language rather than a list of exceptions. Adding nōn to it gives two negatives that cancel, which is M3's nisi nōn error and L3-M5's negat sē nōn venīre error — three modules of the same mistake on three different words.

FIVE CONJUNCTIONS NOW REQUIRE THE SUBJUNCTIVE, FOR FIVE DIFFERENT REASONS: ut and nē for purpose (L3-M4), licet for a concession (M4), an for something unknown (M5), cum for a time clause in the past, and dōnec for a thing still to come. The mood is not doing one job in Latin — it is what a whole set of words demand — and a sentence can easily carry three of them at once for three unrelated reasons.

THE TIME WORDS OF THE COURSE NOW SPLIT THREE WAYS. Caseless adverbs that never decline: cotīdiē, crās, herī, hodiē, iam, nōndum. The time ablative with a number agreeing inside it: hōrā prīmā, hōrā sextā. And conjunctions that join a clause: dum, postquam, antequam (L3-M1), cum and dōnec. Three groups, and nothing about a word's meaning tells you which group it belongs to.

words.note: TWO WORDS, ONE SPELLING. cum plus the ablative is 'with' (L1-M7: cum magistrō); cum plus a SUBJUNCTIVE is 'when'. The case or mood after it decides which.
'When he had come' — the pluperfect subjunctive of veniō. M3 opened this shape for counterfactuals and here it is a plain time clause: the mood is what cum requires, not a hypothetical.
'I was glad' — and this is a shape the course has not taught. It arrives properly at M8; here it is written once because a cum clause in the past needs a past beside it.

sentences.trap: cum here is 'when' and L1-M7's cum is 'with'. Same four letters, same key in the index, two grammars — and the index can only hold one note, so this row's note carries both readings and says which is which. The mood after it is the only signal: a case means 'with', a subjunctive means 'when'.

words.note: TWO WORDS, ONE SPELLING. cum plus the ablative is 'with' (L1-M7: cum magistrō); cum plus a SUBJUNCTIVE is 'when'. The case or mood after it decides which.
'Ill' — aeger, aegra, aegrum. L3-M7's word.
'When I was' — the IMPERFECT subjunctive of sum. M3 opened it for present unreal conditions; here it is what cum requires in a time clause about the past.
'Not', in front of what it denies.
'I was working' — the imperfect, which M8 opens properly. Written here because a cum clause needs a past beside it: labōrābam, labōrābat, veniēbam.

sentences.trap: essem is M3's shape doing M6's job. The mood has nothing counterfactual about it here — 'when I was ill' is a fact — and a learner who met vēnisset and essem in a module about regrets will read this time clause as a hypothetical unless the note says otherwise.

words.note: 'Until', and it takes the INDICATIVE for a plain fact. A subjunctive after it would mean 'until such time as', which this course does not write.
'He came' — the perfect of veniō, and one bar from venit, 'he comes'. An INDICATIVE, because dōnec takes one.
'I wait, I wait for': exspectō 'I wait', exspectāvī 'I waited'. It takes a plain object with no 'for' — English 'expect' is the same word.

sentences.trap: dōnec takes the indicative where cum takes a mood, and both are time clauses. So this module has two time conjunctions with opposite requirements — which is M4's quamquam-and-licet problem on a different pair, and the same answer: learn each with its construction.
sentences.sound: DŌ-nec VĒ-nit, ex-spec-TĀ-vī. The long ō opens the line and the long ā closes it.

words.note: 'Already, now'. It takes no ending and it sits before the verb — and with a perfect it is English's 'has already'.
'He came' — the perfect of veniō. With iam in front it is English's 'has already come'.

sentences.trap: iam plus a perfect is how Latin says 'has already'. The perfect on its own is 'came' and iam adds the 'already' — so English's whole 'has … already' construction is one small word in front of a tense the course has had since L1-M5.

words.note: 'Not yet' — nōn and dum welded together, the sixth word in this course with a negative inside it.
'He came' — the perfect of veniō.
'Until' — and here it DOES take a subjunctive, because the coming has not happened yet. That is the reading this course otherwise avoids, and a future wait is the one place it is unavoidable.
'That he may come' — the present subjunctive of veniō. L3-M4's mood, and dōnec takes it when the thing waited for is still to come.
'I shall wait' — L1-M6's -bō future on exspectō, which is a first-conjugation verb like labōrō.

sentences.trap: dōnec with a subjunctive, which S03's rule said this course does not write — and here it must, because you cannot wait for something in the indicative before it has happened. The rule is 'indicative for a fact, subjunctive for a thing still to come', and S03 taught the first half and this sentence the second.

words.note: TWO WORDS, ONE SPELLING. cum plus the ablative is 'with' (L1-M7: cum magistrō); cum plus a SUBJUNCTIVE is 'when'. The case or mood after it decides which.
'Ill' — aeger, aegra, aegrum. L3-M7's word.
'When I was' — the imperfect subjunctive of sum, which is what cum requires.
'Not yet' — nōn and dum welded together, the sixth word in this course with a negative inside it.
'I was working' — the imperfect, which M8 opens properly. Written here because a cum clause needs a past beside it: labōrābam, labōrābat, veniēbam.
'Now' — and iam is 'already' and 'now' both, with the tense after it deciding. With a present it is 'now'; with a perfect it is 'already'.
'I work': labōrō, labōrat, labōrant. L1-M4's verb.

sentences.trap: iam means 'now' here and 'already' in S04, and the tense beside it is the whole difference. With a present it points at the moment of speaking; with a perfect it points back at something finished — one word, two readings, and no ambiguity because the verb always says which.

words.note: 'Until' — with a subjunctive here, because the coming has not happened yet.
'That he may come' — the present subjunctive of veniō.
'I do not know' — nōn welded onto sciō. M5's word, and the fifth of six negatives inside a word.
'Whether', with a subjunctive after it. M5's word.
'True' — vērum as a neuter adjective. M5's word.
'That it may be' — sum's present subjunctive, required after an.

sentences.trap: Three subjunctives in one sentence and three different reasons: dōnec wants one because the coming is still to come, an wants one because it introduces something unknown, and sit is what an governs. The mood is not doing one job in Latin — it is what a whole set of conjunctions require, and by this module a learner has met five of them.
sentences.sound: DŌ-nec VE-ni-at, ne-SCI-ō an VĒ-rum SIT. Twelve syllables, and the three moods are the last word of each phrase.
